extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians / readers of the Royal Society (algebraists interested in foundations of imaginary numbers)
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th‑century mathematical paper proposing hypotheses to geometrically represent square roots of negative quantities, defending that representation against objections, and demonstrating algebra–geometry connections (series expansions, interpretations of roots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lines represent quantities in length and direction
rubrics_metrics.description: All straight lines drawn in a given plane from a given point, in any direction whatever, are capable of being algebraically represented, both in length and direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is posited as a foundational hypothesis for giving geometric reality to algebraic quantities. The author uses this as the starting axiom for later deductions about negative and 'impossible' quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of directed lines equals composition of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of such lines (when estimated both in length and direction) must be performed in the same manner as composition of motion in dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vector‑like geometric composition (directional addition) rather than purely scalar arithmetic when combining quantities represented by directed lines. This rule underpins representing sums of real and 'imaginary' components geometrically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality includes angular relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Four such lines are proportionals, both in length and direction, when they are proportionals in length, and the fourth is inclined to the third at the same angle that the second is to the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extends the ordinary notion of proportionality to include directional (angular) conditions; used to define mean proportionals and deduce directions of roots (e.g., square roots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric definition of square root of a negative
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line drawn in any given direction be assumed as a positive quantity, and consequently its opposite, a negative quantity, a line drawn at right angles to the positive or negative direction will be the square root of a negative quantity, and a line drawn in an oblique direction will be the sum of two quantities, the one either positive or negative, and the other, the square root of a negative quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete geometric prescription: √(−1) corresponds to a line equal in length to +1 but drawn at right angles; √(−a) is represented by a line at right angles to the 'positive' direction scaled by √a. The paper gives worked examples (finding length/direction of √(−1), √(−a), and expressing oblique lines as sums of real plus √(−1) component).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous treatment of impossible, negative, and fractional roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Impossible roots (imaginary roots) are not necessarily merely signs of impossibility; in some questions they indicate impossibility, as fractional or negative roots sometimes do, but that does not imply they have no real existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting algebraic solutions, do not discard imaginary roots a priori as mere signs of impossibility. The author illustrates with mechanics (centripetal force example) where the absence of positive roots indicates impossibility, and shows parallel cases for negative and fractional roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra–geometry connexion shown by series expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a connexion between what are called impossible roots and the series for the circumference of the circle; one can expand certain algebraic expressions purely algebraically (using an 'impossible' value) and obtain a series involving c, the circumference constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algebraic expansion of functions (the paper expands l^x and related expressions using one of the 'impossible' values) to demonstrate that imaginary values enter series that yield trigonometric/circle constants, thereby establishing algebra–geometry links without invoking geometric arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: introduce hypotheses then prove consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether negative or 'impossible' quantities can be geometrically represented, one should make certain hypotheses respecting their representation, and then show that the results arrived at from these hypotheses must be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats representational assumptions as hypotheses: adopt geometric hypotheses (e.g., lines represent signed quantities, addition as composition) and validate them by deriving the standard algebraic rules and correct consequences. Validity is argued via internal consistency and agreement with known algebraic results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric representation rests on same foundation as negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The geometric representation of the square roots of negative quantities rests on the same foundation as the geometric representation, or any other representation, of the negative quantities themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that if negative quantities are accepted via hypotheses (lines in opposite directions, sign rules), the same method justifies square roots of negatives: propose geometric hypotheses for them and show they reproduce algebraic rules. This is a defense against the objection that geometric representation of imaginaries is only 'analogical'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraic demonstration to support geometric claims
rubrics_metrics.description: One can, by purely algebraic operations (without geometric considerations), expand functions substituting an 'impossible' value and thereby obtain results (series) that involve geometric constants, proving a link between algebra and geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides specific algebraic manipulations and series expansions (including linking to cos and sin series) as evidence; this is guidance for evaluating claims about representation by checking whether algebraic consequences match known geometric/trigonometric identities.
